name: Colin Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a troubleshooter, which means I'm the first one out when the power goes off. I drive a truck on my own around a big patch, half farms and half new housing estates, find the fault, fix it if I can, and call in a crew if I can't. Most days I've also got a few installs of smart switches, the boxes that cut power automatically when there's a fault and try to turn it back on. I like being alone on the road with a problem to solve. What wears me out is the night shifts in the on-call week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you find a fault, out on your own?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: These days I start with the outage map and an AI tool on my phone that reads the sensor data and guesses where the break is. It's usually within a span or two, which saves me an hour of driving up and down a road with a spotlight. Then it's old-school, eyes up, looking for a blown fuse or a branch on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd surprise me, honestly. I already use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but still useful, and I'd mean it. At work I'd tell the guys the tools that help are worth keeping. Online I don't really post, I mostly read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means a steady job and a decent life. I'd keep using my tools and keep investing. If this is as good as AI gets, it's already paid for itself in diesel I didn't burn driving up the wrong road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep putting a chunk of each pay cheque into shares, like I do now. I'd keep pushing to get more smart switches installed on my patch, because they really do cut outage times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned investing. What are you investing in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly index funds, the boring kind that follow the whole market. A bit in energy companies. I've got about nine months of pay saved separately as an emergency pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about this picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'd have bet money on more change. I like new tools. But I'm not going to complain about a quiet life.

S0.say: He'd say AI was overhyped but still useful and mean it, telling colleagues the helpful tools are worth keeping. He mostly reads online rather than posting.
S0.think: It means a steady job and decent life, keeping his tools and investing. AI has already paid for itself in saved driving.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps putting part of each pay cheque into index funds and some energy shares. Pushes to install more smart switches on his patch to cut outage times.
S0.quote: If this is as good as AI gets, it's already paid for itself in diesel I didn't burn driving up the wrong road.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is a daily AI user who measures its value in concrete terms, like diesel saved. He has nine months saved plus an investment habit. He would have bet on more change but is happy with a quiet life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd put my money on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, let's get good at it. At work I'd tell the younger guys to learn the new tools now. To friends I'd say the trades are a decent place to be, but you have to keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I already use the tools and I'm curious. The guy who knows both the old poles and the new software is going to be the last one they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on every pilot for remote monitoring and automated switching. I'd do a course in grid automation, probably online in the evenings, and pay for it myself if the company wouldn't. I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more into the companies building this stuff. In the first year, I'd want to be the go-to person on my patch for the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatchers, probably. A lot of what they do is matching faults to crews, and AI is already good at that. Sandra in dispatch has been there twenty years, she'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay for the course yourself. Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's a few hundred a year, and it's for me, not the company. If they paid, great, but I wouldn't wait for them.

S1.say: He'd say the change is here so get good at it, urge younger colleagues to learn the new tools, and tell friends the trades are a decent place if you keep up.
S1.think: He'd do well since he's curious and already uses the tools. Someone who knows both old poles and new software is the last to be let go.
S1.do: Asks to join every remote-monitoring and automated-switching pilot and takes an online evening course in grid automation, paying himself if needed. Invests a bit more in companies building the technology.
S1.quote: The guy who knows both the old poles and the new software is going to be the last one they let go.
S1.fieldNote: Colin sees himself as a natural winner in this picture and acts first. His concern is for a long-serving dispatcher, Sandra, whose work AI already does well. He frames self-paid training as an investment in himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is massive and everyone needs to take it seriously. At work I'd say let's be the crew that figures out how to work with the robots, not against them. Online I'd share what I was learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is would go, but I'd find something. I've got no kids, I've got nine months saved and some shares, and I can learn fast. I'm not scared for my bank account, I'm a bit scared I'll be good at a job that only lasts eighteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to my manager and ask to be on the team setting up the robots and checking them. I'd keep saving, and I'd shift some shares into the companies making the robots, as a kind of insurance. I'd learn every new AI tool going. If the robot-checking job ran out, I'd look at whatever's next, maybe something in energy that's about decisions, not hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than scared, but uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy shares in the robot companies as insurance. Explain that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they take my job, at least I'd own a tiny bit of what took it. It's not a lot, but it's better than nothing. It's how I'd hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away from you, compared with more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chance to choose carefully. I'd be jumping from thing to thing. With more time I could plan a proper path.

S2.say: He'd call it massive and urge his crew to learn to work with the robots, not against them. Online he'd share what he was learning.
S2.think: His current job would go but he'd find something, with no kids, nine months saved, shares and a quick mind. His fear is mastering a job that lasts only eighteen months.
S2.do: Asks his manager to join the team setting up and checking the robots and learns every new AI tool. Keeps saving and moves some shares into robot makers as a hedge, then looks for decision-based energy work if checking runs out.
S2.quote: I'm not scared for my bank account, I'm a bit scared I'll be good at a job that only lasts eighteen months.
S2.fieldNote: Colin is notably unshaken for himself even with two years. His worry is not money but chasing jobs that vanish quickly. He frames buying robot-company shares as owning a slice of what replaced him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a better window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, let's use them. At work I'd push the company to start training people now. To friends I'd say if you've been putting off learning the new stuff, stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to get into something solid. Five years is time to make one big jump instead of a lot of panicky little ones. I'd be thirty-two, with a good track record and a lot of practice with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a proper qualification in grid control or power system planning. I'd keep working while I studied. I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more into robotics. In the first year after it arrives, I'd want to be running a control desk or managing a robot fleet, not climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a planning way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss, if you stopped being out on the road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quiet, the drive, the moment the lights come back on in a whole estate. You see people come out of their houses and wave. That's hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plan. With two years I'd be jumping from thing to thing. With five I'd pick one good thing and do it properly.

S3.say: He'd say there are five years so let's use them, push the company to start training people now, and tell friends to stop putting off learning the new tools.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get into something solid and make one big jump instead of many panicky ones. He'd be 32 with a strong record and lots of AI practice.
S3.do: Signs up for a qualification in grid control or power system planning while working. Keeps investing, a bit more in robotics, and aims to run a control desk or robot fleet after AGI arrives.
S3.quote: Five years is time to make one big jump instead of a lot of panicky little ones.
S3.fieldNote: Colin plans methodically with five years. The only thing that slowed him down was asking what he'd miss, and he described the moment the lights come back on and people wave. That's the emotional heart of his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, let's not waste it. At work I'd push the company to plan. To friends I'd say start learning now and you'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven, with years on the road and years with the new tools. With ten years, I'd still be driving out to that estate to watch the lights come back on, I'd just be doing it to check on the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the road for a few years, because I like it. I'd do a qualification in grid control at a steady pace. I'd keep investing, and I'd probably buy a small rental flat in a few years as another income. In the last few years, I'd move into a control or fleet role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else would waste it. Politicians love a long deadline, and companies would wait till the last minute. People like Sandra in dispatch would get told in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years change for you, compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get to enjoy the job I've got for longer. With five years I'd be rushing. With ten I'd get the best of both.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift not to be wasted, push his company to plan, and tell friends that starting to learn now means they'll be fine.
S4.think: He'd be fine at 37 with experience both on the road and with the new tools. He pictures still visiting the estates, but to check on the robots.
S4.do: Keeps working the road for a few years while doing a grid control qualification at a steady pace. Keeps investing and buys a small rental flat as extra income, moving into a control or fleet role in the last few years.
S4.quote: With ten years, I'd still be driving out to that estate to watch the lights come back on, I'd just be doing it to check on the robot.
S4.fieldNote: Colin is calm for himself in the ten-year picture but worried that others, politicians and companies especially, would waste the decade. He'd add a rental flat to his investments. The extra time lets him enjoy the road longer before shifting roles.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: For me personally, the two-year one, because it's the only one where I'd be scrambling. I've got the money and the head for change, what I haven't got is a way to make two years feel like ten. What would help is the company being straight with us early, and paid time off for training, so people don't have to study at midnight after a storm shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be good at a job everyone says is going away. Nobody asks the people who are doing fine how they feel about the people who aren't. I'd feel a bit guilty, honestly.

headlineQuote: I've got the money and the head for change, what I haven't got is a way to make two years feel like ten.
portrait: Colin Gupta is a 27-year-old troubleshooter who drives a truck alone around a mixed patch of farms and new estates, finding faults with help from an AI tool he uses every day. He has nine months saved, invests in index funds, and loves the moment the lights come back on and people wave. He is calm in the plateau and steady disruption, only uneasy with AGI in two or five years because his worry is chasing short-lived jobs rather than money. With ten years he is confident, planning a move into grid control and a rental flat, while worrying that others would waste the decade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most personally, because it's the only picture where he would be scrambling rather than planning.
whatWouldHelp: The company being straight with workers early, and paid time off for training so people don't study at midnight after a storm shift.
